summary: Vision is an autonomous observatory for public SPHEREx data. SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, but its archive is too large to inspect by hand. Vision watches the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive on its own: it finds newly released exposures, downloads and validates them, measures every source with error bars, and builds wavelength-aware spectra, light curves and motion tracks. Three discovery engines flag moving, variable and spectrally unusual sources, and a transparent Bayesian classifier, checked against Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD, estimates what each one most likely is — for example, the nearby brown dwarf Epsilon Indi B comes out as a brown-dwarf candidate at over 99%. A local open-weight AI model then explains each result in plain language, without any cloud AI service, and it is never allowed to invent numbers or claim a discovery. Every result links back to the real exposures, which researchers can step through frame by frame. Vision turns a flood of public data into honest, traceable leads that people can check for themselves.
details:
What it does. Vision is a full-stack platform that runs on its own:

  1. Monitor: every 6 hours it asks the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive which SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images cover its monitored fields. If the archive's TAP query service is down, it falls back to the SIA2 image-search service. Exposures that are already known are downloaded continuously in small, polite batches as cutouts. Each file is checksummed, stored read-only and validated before use.
    • It reads the WCS, flag, variance, ePSF and WCS-WAVE extensions of every exposure.
    • It detects sources and runs forced aperture photometry with PSF corrections and uncertainties.
    • It builds spectra over the 102 SPHEREx channels. Because each exposure sees only one wavelength, colour is never mistaken for variability.
    • It builds template-normalised light curves and fits proper motion from per-exposure centroids.
    • It cross-matches SIMBAD, Gaia DR3 and SkyBoT at the epoch of each observation.
  2. Discover: three engines flag moving-object, variable and spectral-anomaly candidates. Each candidate uses fixed, documented criteria and shows its evidence, its confidence grade and its limitations. A candidate is never presented as a confirmed discovery.
    • Evidence: water and methane band indices, colour temperature, infrared excess, source extent, variability, Gaia parallax and SIMBAD types.
    • Self-check: from photometry alone it recognises 37 of 38 Gaia-confirmed Milky Way objects and gets the exact type right for 6 of 6 SIMBAD-identified sources. Because these same sources were used to tune two settings, the interface labels this as a partly in-sample check.
    • every number is copied from the analysis engine;
    • text containing numbers that cannot be traced to a measurement is rejected;
    • the model cannot raise a confidence grade;
    • it cannot claim a discovery.
  3. Improve: researchers review interpretations. Reviewed examples become a versioned dataset for LoRA fine-tuning (PEFT) with held-out evaluation and rollback. Training never starts automatically.

What you see. A web interface with ten pages, in English and Turkish:

  • Overview and Observatory: monitoring status.
  • Discoveries: each candidate has a "What could it be?" probability panel and the real SPHEREx exposures behind the result, playable frame by frame.
  • Research targets: five validation objects (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis).
  • Sky explorer: a live archive search for any position.
  • Time-lapse viewer, Spectral analysis, Vision AI, Research archive and Settings.

Benefits and impact. Vision lets students, amateur and professional astronomers explore a new NASA all-sky survey without writing archive queries. It surfaces leads such as brown-dwarf candidates and variable young stars, and it shows exactly how each lead was reached and how strong the evidence is. It is honest by design: when data are missing or unreliable it says so. For example, three of the five targets are too bright for SPHEREx photometry, and the system reports this rather than producing numbers.

Tools and technologies.

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy/Alembic (SQLite or PostgreSQL).
  • Astronomy: Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, photutils.
  • Numerics and machine learning: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (Isolation Forest).
  • Local AI: PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and PEFT, Sentence Transformers, FAISS.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, with hand-written SVG charts.
  • Deployment and tests: Docker Compose; 38 automated tests.
  • Hardware: a Windows laptop (Intel i5, 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti 4 GB).

Creativity. The language model never produces the numbers or the probabilities. Physics-based measurement and a transparent classifier produce them; the model only explains. This separation makes the AI's statements checkable. The interface is designed as an editorial "research instrument" rather than a generic dashboard, and the viewer links every claim back to the raw images.

Factors we considered.

  • Scientific honesty: no fabricated data, explicit uncertainty and limitations.
  • SPHEREx specifics: 6.15″ pixels and blending, one wavelength per exposure, saturation of bright stars.
  • Proper motion of nearby stars, so that a moving star is not mistaken for a solar-system object.
  • Archive outages, which led to the SIA2 fallback, retries and caching.
  • Politeness to public services.
  • Running entirely on modest local hardware, with no external AI API.
